hints: Think of concentrated sulfuric acid as a strong acid donating a proton to the chloride ion to make hydrogen chloride gas, leaving a hydrogensulfate salt behind.
walkthrough:
Picture the proton transfer**
Imagine solid $\text{NaCl}$ meeting concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$. The acid gives one $\text{H}^{+}$ to $\text{Cl}^{-}$ to make gaseous $\text{HCl}$. What is left is $\text{Na}^{+}$ joined to $\text{HSO}_{4}^{-}$, so the salt product is sodium hydrogensulfate, $\text{NaHSO}_{4}$.

Write the balanced equation**
Put it together in a 1:1 ratio: $$\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_{4} + \text{HCl}$$ This is balanced for all atoms and shows the steamy white fumes of $\text{HCl}$ forming at room temperature.

hints: Focus on what changes in oxidation number here, nothing is oxidised or reduced, a stronger acid simply displaces a weaker, more volatile acid from its salt.
walkthrough:
Check for redox**
Look at oxidation numbers. In $\text{Cl}^{-}$ to $\text{HCl}$, chlorine stays at -1. In $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ to $\text{HSO}_{4}^{-}$, sulfur stays at +6. Because nothing is oxidised or reduced, this cannot be a redox reaction.

Name the proton transfer**
This is simply a stronger, non-volatile acid displacing a weaker, volatile acid from its salt. Sulfuric acid donates a proton to chloride, so call it an acid-base reaction, also accepted as a displacement reaction.

hints: Remember that sodium iodide first behaves just like sodium chloride, forming its own hydrogen halide which fumes in moist air.
walkthrough:
Apply the same first step**
Just like with $\text{NaCl}$, concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ first protonates $\text{I}^{-}$: $$\text{NaI} + \text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_{4} + \text{HI}$$ So $\text{HI}$ gas is made first.

Link to the observation**
$\text{HI}$, like $\text{HCl}$, is a colourless gas that reacts with moisture in the air to give tiny droplets of acid. That is what you see as steamy fumes, so the chemical responsible is hydrogen iodide, $\text{HI}$.

hints: Recall the characteristic appearance of solid iodine formed when iodide is oxidised.
Think about what concentrated sulfuric acid is reduced to when it oxidises a strong reducing agent like iodide, sulfur can go from +6 to +4, 0 or -2.
walkthrough:
Spot the oxidation of iodide**
$\text{HI}$ made in the first step does not survive. Iodide, $\text{I}^{-}$, is a powerful reducing agent and is oxidised to $\text{I}_{2}$: $$2\text{I}^{-} \rightarrow \text{I}_{2} + 2e^{-}$$ Solid iodine appears as a dark grey or black solid that gives purple vapour on warming.

Spot the reduction of sulfuric acid**
At the same time concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ acts as an oxidising agent and is itself reduced. With a strong reducer like iodide it can be reduced all the way to $\text{SO}_{2}$ (sulfur +4), to $\text{S}$ (sulfur 0), to $\text{H}_{2}\text{S}$ (sulfur -2), with $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ also formed. Any one of $\text{S}$, $\text{H}_{2}\text{S}$ or $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ is an acceptable other product.

Final answer: dark grey solid: iodine, $\text{I}_{2}$
other product: sulfur, $\text{S}$ OR hydrogen sulfide, $\text{H}_{2}\text{S}$ OR water, $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

hints: Compare the observations, white steamy fumes only for chloride versus steamy fumes plus coloured solids and pungent gases for iodide.
Link this difference to the ability of $\text{Cl}^{-}$ versus $\text{I}^{-}$ to donate electrons to concentrated sulfuric acid.
walkthrough:
Contrast what you actually see**
With $\text{NaCl}$ you see only white steamy fumes of $\text{HCl}$ and the reaction stops there. With $\text{NaI}$ you see steamy fumes of $\text{HI}$ at first, then further changes: dark grey solid $\text{I}_{2}$, plus yellow solid sulfur or rotten egg smelling $\text{H}_{2}\text{S}$ and $\text{SO}_{2}$. That tells you something extra is happening for iodide.

Explain with reducing strength**
The extra step is redox. $\text{I}^{-}$ is larger than $\text{Cl}^{-}$ with its outer electron further from the nucleus and more easily lost, so iodide is a much stronger reducing agent than chloride. Concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ is strong enough to oxidise $\text{HI}$ / $\text{I}^{-}$ to $\text{I}_{2}$, itself being reduced, but it is not strong enough to oxidise $\text{HCl}$ / $\text{Cl}^{-}$, so the chloride reaction remains simple acid-base only.

Final answer: Iodide ions are stronger reducing agents than chloride ions.
$\text{HI}$ / iodide is oxidised by concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ whereas $\text{HCl}$ / chloride is not oxidised.

hints: Remember bromide is an intermediate reducing agent, it reduces sulfuric acid to sulfur dioxide while being oxidised to bromine.
walkthrough:
Identify the redox pair**
Bromide sits between chloride and iodide in reducing power. It is oxidised: $$2\text{Br}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Br}_{2} + 2e^{-}$$ Sulfuric acid is reduced from S(+6) to S(+4) in $\text{SO}_{2}$.

Complete the given skeleton**
Filling the coefficients to balance atoms and charge gives: $$2\text{Br}^{-} + 2\text{H}^{+} + \text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} \rightarrow \text{Br}_{2} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \text{SO}_{2}$$ Check: Br, H, S and O all balance, and the total charge on the left ($-2 + 2 = 0$) matches the neutral products.
